title: Who pays for a tweet?
teaches: Fan-out on write and on read, the hybrid for accounts with millions of followers, and IDs that sort by time
summary: **Optimise for the dominant operation.** When reads outnumber writes sixty to one, precomputing timelines once at write time requires far less total work than assembling them on every read.
**Fan-out on write maintains a cached list per reader.** The system pushes each new tweet's ID into every follower's Redis list, reducing a timeline read to a single list lookup.
**Fan-out on read merges timelines on demand.** Writes require only a single insert, but every read must query hundreds of accounts and wait for the slowest response.
**High-fan-out outliers break write-time designs.** A single tweet from an account with 30 million followers triggers 30 million list inserts and minutes of replication lag.
**A hybrid design separates normal accounts from outliers.** Ordinary accounts are fanned out on write, while high-follower accounts are merged in when a timeline is read.
**Only precompute caches for active readers.** Twitter held timelines in RAM only for recently active users and rebuilt timelines on demand for returning users.

**Snowflake IDs sort by time without per-ID coordination.** Packing 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of worker ID and 12 bits of sequence counter allows each server to allocate up to 4,096 time-ordered IDs per millisecond.
**Generators must halt if the local clock steps backwards.** Issuing IDs with a previously used millisecond timestamp risks duplicate IDs and breaks chronological ordering.

blocks.text: In 2008 Twitter was famous for being down. The site had launched in July 2006 as a Ruby on Rails application on a MySQL database, and it grew faster than anyone had planned for. During big events, when everyone posted at once, the site regularly came to a stop. Visitors then saw a page with a whale held aloft by a flock of small birds, drawn by the designer Yiying Lu.[^whale] Users named it the Fail Whale, and it became the best-known error page on the web.

Much of the load came from one page. A user's home timeline shows the latest tweets from everyone they follow, newest first. In the first design, the system built this timeline on demand whenever a user requested it by finding the accounts the user followed, fetching their recent tweets, sorting them and keeping the top twenty. That is a query across hundreds of accounts, run every time anyone opens the app or refreshes the page.

In November 2012, at the QCon conference in San Francisco, Raffi Krikorian, who had led Twitter's platform engineering, described the replacement architecture in a talk called "Timelines at Scale". The engineers faced a central design choice between doing the work of building a timeline when a tweet is written or doing it when a timeline is read.

Before choosing, we can look at the rounded numbers from Krikorian's talk: users wrote about **5,000 tweets a second** on average, and made about **300,000 timeline reads a second**. Reads outnumber writes sixty to one. For the arithmetic, we can assume two more round numbers: a tweet's author has about 200 followers, and a reader follows about 200 accounts.

With **fan-out on read**, the system does the work at read time, as the first design did. A tweet is written once, giving 5,000 writes a second. Each timeline read gathers tweets from 200 accounts, which requires 300,000 × 200 = 60 million lookups a second. With **fan-out on write**, the system does the work at write time. It inserts each tweet's ID into the cached timeline of each of its author's followers, requiring 5,000 × 200 = 1 million inserts a second, and each read then fetches one ready-made list.

blocks.caption: The work of each design, in a model built from the numbers above; the bars are on a log scale. The last row is one tweet from the account with the most followers, showing how many timeline inserts it needs. Inserts are assumed to run at 100,000 a second for one tweet. In the hybrid, accounts with over 1 million followers are not pushed, and a reader is assumed to follow 3 of them, so a read fetches 4 lists.
blocks.task: Guess first. Then raise the biggest account to 30 million followers and find the design that neither floods the inserts nor slows every read.

blocks.text: Fan-out on write requires about 1.3 million operations a second compared to 60 million operations a second for fan-out on read. That is roughly fifty times less work, because the work done once per tweet is shared across the many reads of each timeline. Reads also have lower and more predictable tail latency. A read that gathers data from 200 servers must wait for the slowest server, and as we saw in lesson 9, if 1% of servers are slow at a given moment, about 87% of such reads will wait on at least one slow server.

Twitter stored its timelines in Redis, an in-memory database with a native list data structure, distributed across a cluster of machines. Each user's home timeline was a list of at most **800** entries, each holding a tweet's ID and a few bytes of metadata, rather than the tweet's text. When a user posted a tweet, a fan-out service queried a social graph service (called Flock) for the author's followers and appended the ID to each follower's list, trimming the oldest entry. Twitter replicated each list across **three** machines, so losing one machine lost no timelines. A timeline read fetched the IDs from one list and then looked up the tweets themselves from a separate tweet store, mostly hitting its cache (as in lesson 5).

The memory, in round numbers: 150 million active users × 800 IDs × 8 bytes is about 1 TB, three copies make 3 TB, before Redis's own overhead. That fits in the memory of a modest cluster. It would not have fitted for every account ever created, so timelines were kept only for users who had logged in within the last 30 days. A returning user's timeline was rebuilt from the tweet store when they came back, by the slow path, once.[^inactive]

Fan-out on write is a precomputed cache (whereas lesson 5 built caches on demand), so it inherits the consistency problems of caching. Every change to a timeline must be written in many places: if a user deletes a tweet, the system must either remove it from every list it was pushed to, or filter it out when a timeline is read. Followers also see a tweet at slightly different times, since the fan-out writes to their lists one by one. Because a large fan-out is a long job, workers process it asynchronously from a message queue (lesson 16). If a worker crashes after completing 10 million of 30 million inserts, another worker retries the job. The retry repeats those 10 million inserts, which is safe provided the insert operation is idempotent, checking whether the tweet ID is already in the list and skipping it.

Average follower counts hide the accounts that strain the system most. If we increase one author's followers from 200 to 30 million, a factor of 150,000 (as Lady Gaga's account had reached by late 2012), a single tweet requires 30 million inserts. That equals the write volume the entire cluster handles in 30 seconds at its normal rate of 1 million inserts a second. A single tweet's fan-out cannot consume the entire cluster's throughput, either. At an assumed rate of 100,000 inserts a second for a single tweet, as in the figure, the fan-out takes 300 seconds. Krikorian noted that a tweet from a high-follower account could take minutes to reach every follower's timeline, meaning early recipients would reply to a tweet that other followers could not yet see, violating causal ordering.

A **hybrid** design handles these high-follower outliers separately. Accounts below a follower threshold use fan-out on write as before. Twitter adjusted this threshold over time (for example, using tens of thousands of followers); the figure above uses 1 million. Engineers tune the threshold by measuring the queue latency of the largest fan-outs and lowering the limit until fan-outs complete within an acceptable delay. Tweets from accounts above the threshold are not fanned out on write at all. Instead, when a user reads their timeline, the service fetches their precomputed list and merges it at read time with the recent tweets of the high-follower accounts they follow. A read then fetches a handful of lists instead of one, and a tweet from a large account becomes visible to all its followers simultaneously. Set the biggest account in the figure above to 30 million followers and compare the three designs.

When designing for skewed workloads, we optimise for the read-to-write ratio of the common case, and handle extreme outliers with a separate code path. The same pattern appears whenever a few keys receive far more traffic than the rest, such as the row-key hot spots in lesson 10.

A timeline stores tweet IDs and must keep them in chronological order, which is much simpler if the IDs themselves sort by time. MySQL's `AUTO_INCREMENT` column assigned sequential IDs, but only because a single database coordinated every write. When Twitter began migrating tweets to the distributed database Cassandra (lesson 12), which has no central counter, engineers needed a way for many servers to generate time-ordered IDs independently. On 1 June 2010, the Twitter engineering blog announced **Snowflake**, a service that generates 64-bit IDs composed of a sign bit and three fields.

blocks.title: A Snowflake ID, from the top bit down
points: One unused sign bit, set to 0 so the 64-bit signed integer remains positive.
41 bits for the timestamp in [[milliseconds|clock]] since a custom epoch, giving a range of 69 years.[^epoch]
10 bits for the worker ID (5 bits for datacentre ID and 5 bits for machine ID), allowing 1,024 generators to run concurrently without collisions as long as each has a unique ID.
12 bits for a per-millisecond [[sequence|request]] number, allowing one generator to allocate up to 4,096 IDs within a single millisecond.

blocks.text: Because the timestamp occupies the most significant bits, an ID generated in a later millisecond is numerically larger than any ID from an earlier millisecond, regardless of which machine generated it. Sorting by ID therefore sorts by time, accurate to within the clock skew between machines. Worker IDs are the only point of coordination: each generator is assigned its worker ID at deployment and registers it with ZooKeeper (an open-source coordination service similar to lesson 11's Chubby) at start-up to ensure no two servers share an ID. After start-up, generators never communicate with one another to issue an ID, making generation as fast as incrementing a local counter and resilient to network partitions.

blocks.caption: One Snowflake generator over 20 ms, as a time lapse. Each column is one millisecond, showing [[IDs handed out|answer]], [[requests waiting|busy]] for the next millisecond, and [[requests refused|error]], which happens only when the clock steps back. The bar at the top shows the latest ID's three fields.
blocks.task: Push the requests past 4,096 a millisecond, then make the clock step back and play past 10 ms.

blocks.text: The figure illustrates two operational limits. First, a single worker can allocate at most 4,096 IDs per millisecond (about 4.1 million IDs a second); if more requests arrive within that millisecond, they must queue until the next millisecond tick. Second, the algorithm relies on the server's wall clock moving monotonically forward. If NTP (lesson 13) steps the local clock backwards to correct drift, the generator could reuse a timestamp from a millisecond it has already exhausted, risking duplicate IDs and breaking chronological order. To prevent this, a Snowflake worker tracks its last used timestamp and refuses to generate IDs if the system clock reads an earlier time, waiting until the clock catches up. This design trades a brief availability outage on that worker for guaranteed ID uniqueness.[^idstr]
Each architecture shifts the computational and storage cost to a different part of the system.

blocks.title: The trade, named
points: Fan-out on write: reads have low, predictable latency from a single list lookup, while writes pay O(N) inserts per follower, RAM must hold every active user's timeline, and deletes must clean up or filter every copy.

Fan-out on read: writes are a single database insert and timelines are immediately consistent, while every read pays for querying hundreds of accounts and suffers the tail latency of the slowest lookup.
The hybrid: engineers must maintain and debug both write-time and read-time paths, in exchange for bounded write fan-out and fast reads across both ordinary and high-follower accounts.
Snowflake: servers generate time-ordered IDs with zero per-request coordination, in exchange for ordering accuracy bounded by NTP clock skew and brief unavailability when a clock steps backwards.

blocks.text: Other engineering teams have arrived at similar designs based on their own workloads. In 2012, Instagram published its ID generation scheme, which packed 41 bits of millisecond timestamp, 13 bits of logical shard ID and 10 bits of auto-incrementing sequence into a 64-bit integer generated directly inside each PostgreSQL shard. Social feeds generally use fan-out on write when reads outnumber writes by an order of magnitude or more, and switch to fan-out on read for high-fan-out accounts where pushing every post would saturate the write queues.

blocks.caption: Six questions on fan-out and IDs
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A service sees 300,000 timeline reads a second and 5,000 posts a second, with an average of 200 followers per author. Why does fan-out on write perform fewer total operations?
choices: Writes are cheaper than reads on every kind of storage, so moving work from reads to writes always reduces load
Each post's fan-out is computed once at write time and amortised across all subsequent reads of each timeline
Fan-out on write stores each tweet only once, while fan-out on read must copy the full tweet text to every follower
items.why: Fan-out on write performs 5,000 × 200 = 1 million inserts a second, plus 300,000 single-list reads a second. Fan-out on read performs 300,000 × 200 = 60 million lookups a second because reads outnumber writes sixty to one.

items.ask: Why did Twitter maintain cached timelines in Redis only for users active within the last 30 days?
choices: Inactive users' timelines consume RAM and write fan-out throughput without being read
Redis cannot hold more than a fixed number of lists on one machine, regardless of how short each list is
Inactive users have no followers, so their timelines would always be empty and cost nothing to skip
items.why: Precomputing and storing a cache in RAM is only worthwhile if the cached data will be read; a rare returning user pays a one-time latency penalty to rebuild their timeline from the backing store.

items.ask: One account has 30 million followers. What fails under pure fan-out on write when this account posts?
choices: Its followers' timelines overflow, since each list holds only 800 entries and its tweets push out all other posts
Each of its tweets must be read 30 million times from the tweet store during fan-out, overloading the cache
The post generates 30 million Redis list inserts, saturating the fan-out queues and taking minutes to reach all followers
items.why: Write work and queue delay scale linearly with the author's follower count; the hybrid design avoids this bottleneck by merging high-follower accounts at read time instead.

items.ask: In the hybrid timeline design, what steps does the service perform on a timeline read?
choices: It queries the recent tweets of every account the reader follows at read time
It fetches the reader's precomputed list and merges in the recent tweets of any high-follower accounts they follow
It fetches the reader's precomputed list only, since high-follower accounts' tweets are pushed via a low-priority background queue
items.why: Ordinary accounts are fanned out on write; only the high-follower outliers are queried on read, so a timeline read fetches and merges a small number of lists.

items.ask: What property does a 64-bit Snowflake ID provide that a random 64-bit ID does not?
choices: IDs sort approximately by creation time and can be generated without network coordination per ID
A guarantee that IDs are strictly consecutive integers, with no gaps between one tweet and the next
Automatic protection against two machines being configured with the same worker ID if ZooKeeper is bypassed
items.why: The time is in the top bits. Coordination happens once, when a machine gets its number; making each ID needs none. IDs leave gaps.

items.ask: A Snowflake generator's local system clock is stepped backwards by 4 ms by NTP. How does the generator respond?
choices: It continues generating IDs using the new clock time, since the 10-bit worker ID keeps its IDs globally unique
It permanently adds a 4 ms offset to all future timestamps so that it never observes the backward step
It refuses requests to generate IDs until the system clock advances past the last millisecond timestamp it used
items.why: Reusing a past millisecond timestamp on the same worker resets the sequence counter and could produce duplicate IDs, as well as out-of-order timestamps; rejecting requests briefly preserves uniqueness and ordering.

whale.title: A greeting card
whale.text: Yiying Lu originally drew the illustration, titled "Lifting a Dreamer", as a birthday greeting card for a friend and uploaded it to the stock-image site iStockphoto. Twitter licensed it there for its over-capacity error page. Lu only learned how Twitter was using her drawing when users began talking about the Fail Whale.

inactive.title: Two paths anyway
inactive.text: Because inactive users' timelines are rebuilt by querying the accounts they follow, fan-out on write never eliminates the read-time assembly path; it just makes that path rare. Any architecture that caches only the active working set still has to maintain the uncached query path, and must provision it to survive traffic spikes when many inactive users return during a major event.

epoch.title: Twitter's epoch
epoch.text: Counting from the standard Unix epoch of 1 January 1970 would have wasted the first 40 years of the 41-bit timestamp field, so Snowflake counts from a custom epoch (`twepoch`) of 1288834974657 in Unix milliseconds, corresponding to 01:42:54 UTC on 4 November 2010. A 41-bit unsigned integer holds 2^41 - 1 milliseconds, or about 69.7 years, which overflows in September 2080.

idstr.title: Too big for JavaScript
idstr.text: JavaScript represents all numbers as IEEE 754 double-precision (64-bit) floats, which can represent integers with exact precision only up to 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992). Snowflake IDs exceed 2^53, so web browsers parsing Twitter's JSON responses silently rounded the least significant digits. To prevent corruption, Twitter added an `id_str` field to its API responses containing the exact ID formatted as a string.
